Random variables and expected value

Is the spinner at the Christmas market worth it? Is an extended warranty worth its money? In random experiments you are often interested in a number: the total score, the win in euros, the number of hits. Such numbers are called random variables. Their expected value tells you what you can count on in the long run.

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • describe random variables and give their probability distribution as a table and a chart
  • calculate and interpret the expected value
  • distinguish the chance of winning from the expected win, recognise fair games
  • simulate random experiments and estimate risks

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Random variables and their distribution

When you roll two dice there are 36 equally likely pairs. The total score assigns a number to every pair: $(3, 4)$ gets the 7. The 7 comes from six pairs, the 2 from only one. That is why $P(\text{total } 7) = \tfrac{6}{36}$ and $P(\text{total } 2) = \tfrac{1}{36}$.

KEY POINT · RANDOM VARIABLE

A random variable $X$ assigns a number to every outcome of a random experiment: the total score, the number of hits, the win in euros.

Its probability distribution states with which probability $X$ takes each value – as a table or a bar chart. All the probabilities together add up to 1.

Multi-stage experiments: path rule (multiply along a path), sum rule (add the paths that lead to the same value).

Complementary event: “at least once” is often quickest to calculate as 1 minus “not at all”.

INTERACTIVE · DISTRIBUTIONS WHEN ROLLING TWO DICE

Choose a random variable. Tap a cell of the table or a bar: the matching pairs of dice light up.

EXAMPLE 1 · THE NUMBER OF SIXES

A dice is rolled twice, $X$ counts the sixes. Give the distribution.

$P(X = 0) = \tfrac{25}{36}$, $\;P(X = 1) = 2 \cdot \tfrac16 \cdot \tfrac56 = \tfrac{10}{36}$, $\;P(X = 2) = \tfrac{1}{36}$. Sum 1.

EXAMPLE 2 · WITHOUT REPLACEMENT

An urn contains 3 red and 2 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. How likely is it that both are red?

$\tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac24 =$ $\tfrac{3}{10}$. With replacement it would be $\tfrac{9}{25}$.

EXERCISES

Two dice: calculate $P(\text{total } 8)$ and $P(\text{double})$.

$\tfrac{5}{36}$ and $\tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac16$

$X$ takes the values 0, 1, 2 with $P(X = 0) = 0.2$ and $P(X = 1) = 0.5$. What is $P(X = 2)$?

$1 - 0.2 - 0.5 = 0.3$

A coin is tossed three times, $X$ counts heads. Give the distribution.

$\tfrac18$, $\tfrac38$, $\tfrac38$, $\tfrac18$ for 0, 1, 2, 3.

How likely is at least one 6 in two rolls?

$1 - \tfrac{25}{36} = \tfrac{11}{36}$. Not $\tfrac16 + \tfrac16$, or the double six is counted twice.

When rolling two dice, $Y$ is the larger score. Find $P(Y = 6)$ and $P(Y = 1)$.

$P(Y = 6) = 1 - \tfrac{25}{36} = \tfrac{11}{36}$, $P(Y = 1) = \tfrac{1}{36}$.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Expected value and fair games

With the spinner you win €3 in one case out of six (€4 payout minus €1 stake), otherwise you lose €1. In 600 rounds that is about 100 wins and 500 losses: $100 \cdot 3 - 500 \cdot 1 = -200$ euros. So per round you lose about 33 cents on average.

KEY POINT · EXPECTED VALUE

$E(X) = x_1 \cdot P(X = x_1) + x_2 \cdot P(X = x_2) + \ldots$ – every value times its probability, all added up.

The expected value is the mean in the long run. In a single trial it often does not occur at all.

A game is fair if the expected value of the win is zero: expected payout = stake.

Chance is not expectation: a 90% chance of winning €1, but a 10% risk of losing €20: $E = 0.9 - 2 = -1.10$ euros.

Roulette: 37 numbers, one number pays €36. $E = \tfrac{36}{37} - 1 \approx -2.7$ cents per euro.

INTERACTIVE · BUILDING A FAIR GAME

Change the stake and the payouts until the expected value of the win is zero.

EXAMPLE 3 · THE SPINNER

A spinner pays nothing with $\tfrac12$, €2 with $\tfrac14$ and €4 with $\tfrac14$. A spin costs €2. Is the game fair?

Expected payout $0 + 0.5 + 1 = 1.50$ euros, win $-0.50$ euros per spin: not fair.

EXAMPLE 4 · MAKING IT FAIR

Stake €1, roll once, there is money only for a 6. How high must the payout be for the game to be fair?

$A \cdot \tfrac16 = 1$ euro, so $A = 6$ euros.

EXERCISES

Calculate the expected value of the score of a fair dice.

$\tfrac{1 + 2 + \ldots + 6}{6} = 3.5$

$X$ takes the values 0, 10 and 20 with the probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2. Calculate $E(X)$.

$0 + 3 + 4 = 7$

In a raffle with 1000 tickets at €2 each there is one prize of €500, ten of €50 and a hundred of €5. Calculate the expected payout and the win per ticket.

$1500 \div 1000 = 1.50$ euros, win $-0.50$ euros per ticket.

Stake €1, two coin tosses, a payout of €3 for two heads. Calculate the expected win. Which payout would be fair?

$3 \cdot \tfrac14 - 1 = -0.25$ euros. Fair at €4.

Game A: a 60% chance of winning €1, otherwise a loss of €2. Game B: a 10% chance of winning €15, otherwise a loss of €2. Which game is better, which is riskier?

A: $0.6 - 0.8 = -0.20$ euros. B: $1.5 - 1.8 = -0.30$ euros. A is better value in the long run, B fluctuates more.

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Simulation and risk

Not every random experiment is easy to calculate. Then a simulation helps: the computer generates random numbers, plays the experiment through thousands of times, and the relative frequencies give estimates of the probabilities.

KEY POINT · SIMULATION AND RISK

Simulating: choose random numbers so that each outcome has the right probability – e.g. the digits 0, 1, 2 for an event with 30%.

Law of large numbers: over many runs the relative frequency approaches the probability.

Risk of damage: probability times the amount of the damage, that is the expected damage.

Components: in series they all have to work ($p^n$). In parallel the system only fails when all of them fail.

Simulating two dice: add two random numbers from 1 to 6 – not one random number from 2 to 12, because the totals are not equally likely.

INTERACTIVE · THE SAME EXPECTED VALUE, A DIFFERENT RISK

Two games with the same expected value: simulate many rounds and compare how strongly the wins fluctuate.

EXAMPLE 5 · THE STRING OF LIGHTS

20 bulbs are connected in series, each works with a probability of 99%. How likely is it that the string lights up?

$0.99^{20} \approx$ 0.818, so only in about 82% of cases.

EXAMPLE 6 · INSURE OR NOT?

A mobile phone is worth €400 and breaks with a probability of 5% per year. Insurance costs €60 a year.

Expected damage $400 \cdot 0.05 =$ €20. On average the insurance is not worth it – but if you could not pay for a repair, you are buying security.

EXERCISES

In 200 simulations an event occurred 38 times. Give the relative frequency. Is that the probability?

$0.19$ – an estimate, not an exact probability.

How do you use random digits 0 to 9 to simulate an event with a probability of 70%?

It occurs for seven of the ten digits, e.g. 0 to 6.

Two pumps work in parallel, each fails with 10%. How likely is it that the system fails? How likely if they were connected in series?

Parallel: $0.1^2 = 1\%$. In series: $1 - 0.9^2 = 19\%$.

A device fails with 2% per year. How likely is it to survive three years? How likely is it to fail at least once in two years?

$0.98^3 \approx 94.1\%$. $1 - 0.98^2 \approx 4\%$.

The Chevalier de Méré bet that he would throw at least one 6 in four rolls. Calculate his probability of winning. Why is $4 \cdot \tfrac16$ wrong?

$1 - \left(\tfrac56\right)^4 \approx 51.8\%$. With $4 \cdot \tfrac16$, rolls with several sixes would be counted more than once.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A dice is rolled 600 times. How many sixes do you expect? Why is exactly 100 rather rare?

About 100. The number fluctuates randomly around 100, exactly 100 is just one value among many.

In roulette with 37 numbers, 18 are red. If you bet €1 on red and win, you get €2. Calculate the expected win.

$2 \cdot \tfrac{18}{37} - 1 \approx -0.027$ euros: the green zero makes the difference.

Repair damage of €120 occurs with 15%, the extended warranty costs €25. Is it worth it on average?

Expected damage €18 < €25: on average, no.

Connecting with learning area 4: an insurance company has 10,000 customers, each has damage of €500 with 1%. What premium does it need at least? Why does it charge more?

Expected damage €5 per customer, €50,000 in total. On top of that come administration, fluctuations and profit.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

A gambler and two letters

The French nobleman Antoine Gombaud, known as the Chevalier de Méré, was a passionate gambler. Among other things he asked the mathematician Blaise Pascal how to divide the stakes fairly if a game has to be broken off early.

In 1654 Pascal exchanged letters about it with Pierre de Fermat. Their idea: you work out what each player would have won on average if the game had continued. This exchange of letters is regarded as the birth of probability theory – and the expected value was there from the very beginning.

Source: correspondence between Pascal and Fermat, 1654; after K. Devlin: The Unfinished Game. Basic Books 2008.
